content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has established four levels of biocontainment precautions for handling biological agents, known as Biosafety Levels (BSL) 1 through 4. These levels are determined based on the relative risk posed to the surrounding environment. As of 2006, there are four defined levels, with an additional intermediate level, BSL-3 Ag, specifically for agricultural hazards. Higher BSL numbers correspond to greater risks to the external environment. At the lowest level, BSL-1, containment may involve only a fume hood equipped with HEPA filters. At the highest level, BSL-4, containment involves isolating the organism using advanced building systems, sealed rooms, sealed containers, personal isolation equipment resembling space suits, and strict entry and decontamination procedures. These facilities also require high levels of security to ensure that only authorized personnel can access areas that could impact the containment zone. BSL-4 facilities are often referred to as hot zones. Biosafety Levels: Biosafety Level 1 (BSL-1): This level is suitable for work involving well-characterized agents that are not known to consistently cause disease in healthy adult humans and pose minimal potential hazard to laboratory personnel and the environment. Laboratories at this level are not separated from general building traffic patterns, and work is typically conducted on open benchtops using standard microbiological practices. Special containment equipment or facility design is not required. Laboratory personnel are trained in the procedures conducted and are supervised by a scientist with general training in microbiology or a related science. BSL-1 is considered a cold zone. Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2): This level is similar to BSL-1 but is designed for work involving agents of moderate potential hazard to personnel and the environment. Differences include: Laboratory personnel receive specific training in handling pathogenic agents and are supervised by competent scientists. Access to the laboratory is restricted when work is being conducted. Extreme precautions are taken with contaminated sharp items. Procedures that may create infectious aerosols or splashes are conducted in biological safety cabinets or other physical containment equipment. BSL-2 is also considered a cold zone. Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3): This level is applicable to facilities where work is conducted with indigenous or exotic agents that may cause serious or potentially lethal diseases through inhalation. Laboratory personnel are specifically trained in handling pathogenic and potentially lethal agents and are supervised by experienced scientists. All procedures involving infectious materials are conducted within biological safety cabinets or other physical containment devices, or by personnel wearing appropriate personal protective equipment. The laboratory has special engineering and design features, such as double-door access zones and sealed penetrations. BSL-3 is considered a neutral or warm zone. Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4): This level is reserved for work with dangerous and exotic agents that pose a high risk of life-threatening disease, often with no available vaccines or treatments (e.g., Ebola virus). Agents with close or identical antigenic relationships to BSL-4 agents are also handled at this level until sufficient data are obtained to confirm whether they can be worked with at a lower level. Laboratory staff receive thorough training in handling extremely hazardous infectious agents and understand the containment functions of standard and special practices, containment equipment, and laboratory design. Access to the laboratory is strictly controlled by the laboratory director. The facility is either in a separate building or a controlled area within a building, completely isolated from other areas. Negative air pressure is maintained to ensure air flows into the room if the barrier is breached, and an airlock is used for personnel entry and exit. All activities are confined to Class III biological safety cabinets or Class II cabinets used with positive-pressure personnel suits ventilated by a life support system. BSL-4 is considered a hot zone, as exposure to microorganisms from this level is likely to result in death. Global Biocontainment Facilities: Australia: Australia operates three BSL-4 laboratories: The Australian Animal Health Laboratory in Geelong, Victoria. The Virology Laboratory of the Queensland Department of Health in Coopers Plains, Queensland. The National High Security Laboratory in North Melbourne, Victoria. Brazil: The Fundação Oswaldo Cruz in Rio de Janeiro operates a BSL-4 facility. Canada: Canada has one BSL-4 facility located at the National Microbiology Laboratory in Winnipeg. France: France maintains a P4 laboratory, the Laboratoire P4 Jean Mérieux, in Lyon. Gabon: The Centre International de Recherches Médicales de Franceville (CIRMF) operates West Africa's only BSL-4 lab. Germany: Germany has two L4 facilities: One at the Philipps University of Marburg, Institute of Virology. The Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg. A new P4 lab is under construction in Marburg, and another is planned at the Robert Koch Institute in Berlin. Japan: Japan has a BSL-4 lab at the National Institute for Infectious Diseases in Tokyo, but it currently operates with BSL-3 agents. Another non-operational BSL-4 lab exists at the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research in Tsukuba. India: India's BSL-4 lab, the High Security Animal Disease Laboratory (HSADL) in Bhopal, handles zoonotic organisms and emerging infectious disease threats. Italy: Italy's only BSL-4 lab is at the Istituto Nazionale Malattie Infettive, Ospedale Lazzaro Spallanzani, in Rome. Russia: The VECTOR State Research Center of Virology and Biotechnology in Koltsovo, Novosibirsk region, is Russia's primary BSL-4 facility. Other Soviet-era BSL-4 facilities have been dismantled. Singapore: The Defence Science Organization (DSO) National Laboratories operates a BSL-4 facility. Singapore also has a mobile BSL-4 autopsy facility, possibly the only one of its kind globally. South Africa: The National Institute for Communicable Diseases, Special Pathogens Unit in Johannesburg, is one of two BSL-4 labs in Africa. Sweden: The Swedish Institute for Infectious Disease Control runs Scandinavia's only P4 laboratory in Solna. Switzerland: The Institute of Virology and Immunoprophylaxis in Mittelhäusern is Switzerland's only publicly known BSL-4 lab, dealing exclusively with animal diseases that do not transmit to humans. A P4 lab was inaugurated in 2007 at the Teaching Hospital of Geneva. Taiwan: Taiwan has two BSL-4 laboratories: The Preventive Medical Institute of the ROC Ministry of National Defense. The Kwen-yang Laboratory, Center of Disease Control, Department of Health. United Kingdom: The UK has three operational BSL-4 laboratories, with another under construction. Existing facilities include: A lab at the National Institute for Medical Research in London. A facility built by the Ministry of Defence at Porton Down, called the Chemical and Biological Defence Establishment. A BSL-4 lab in the Viral Zoonosis unit at the Health Protection Agency's Centre for Infections in Colindale. United States: The United States has at least eight operational BSL-4 facilities and is planning at least seven more. Operational facilities include: USAMRIID in Fort Detrick, MD. CDC in Atlanta, GA (two buildings). NIH's BSL-4 lab in Bethesda, MD (used for training, not as a hot BSL-4). NIH's BSL-4 lab in Rockville, MD. Southwest Foundation for Biomedical Research in San Antonio, TX. UTMB's Shope Laboratory in Galveston, TX. Georgia State University in Atlanta, GA (small glovebox facility). The Division of Consolidated Laboratory Services lab in Richmond, VA (surge BSL-4 capacity). Facilities under construction or planned include: A new USAMRIID building in Fort Detrick, MD. Boston University's National Emerging Infectious Diseases Laboratory (NEIDL) in Boston, MA. UTMB's National Biocontainment Facility in Galveston, TX. DHS's National Biodefense Analysis and Countermeasures Center (NBACC) in Fort Detrick, MD. DHS's National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility (NBAF), with the location to be determined.
